insights.title: Testing is expected from day one
insights.text: 64% of the adverts asked for testing, including every backend advert. That is why you write tests from Chapter 2.

insights.title: Teamwork beats lone genius
insights.text: Teamwork (61%), problem solving (58%) and communication (52%) were the most common asks: pull requests, code review and explaining your work matter as much as code.

insights.title: A degree helps, a portfolio proves
insights.text: Only 39% of adverts strictly required a technical degree; many said "or equivalent experience". Your reviewed projects and Show & Tell videos are your proof.

insights.title: Use AI tools, and explain what they write
insights.text: 22% of adverts mentioned AI coding tools, and a few require them. One South African employer asks juniors to explain AI-written code line by line.

insights.title: Read the experience line, not just the title
insights.text: Several adverts titled "junior" still asked for 1-2 years. Look for intern, graduate, apprentice and trainee roles, and use "You vs a job advert" to check.

insights.title: Africa hires full-stack, Laravel, Java and Flutter
insights.text: Full-stack was the most common junior advert in Africa; PHP/Laravel appeared in 19% of African adverts, Java led backend roles, and Flutter led mobile.

insights.title: Cameroon: few adverts, so look wider
insights.text: We found only a handful of entry-level developer adverts in Cameroon (Douala and Yaoundé), mostly short-lived. Regional employers, remote roles and French skills widen your options.

html_css.example: UK government designers published six posters of accessibility dos and don'ts, one for each user group (for example screen reader users, low-vision users and people with dyslexia). For screen reader users they say to build for keyboard-only use and not to put information only in an image or video.
html_css.source_title: Dos and don'ts on designing for accessibility (Accessibility in government blog, 2 September 2016)

html_css.example: The GOV.UK Service Manual says government services must work using only HTML, because HTML is fault-tolerant, while CSS and especially JavaScript can fail (network errors, ad blockers, firewalls). JavaScript should only enhance a page that already works, so people can still finish their task when it breaks.
html_css.source_title: Building a robust frontend using progressive enhancement (GOV.UK Service Manual)

html_css.company: Nigerian banks and fintech apps (reported by TechCabal)
html_css.example: Blind Nigerian users told TechCabal that many websites and apps have unlabelled buttons, missing alt text, no keyboard navigation and placeholders used instead of form labels, so screen readers cannot read them; one user had to uninstall a bank app after an update made it unusable. OPay was named as an exception because blind users can set up an account on their own through screen reader support.
html_css.source_title: Left behind: The millions of Nigerians whose use of technology is an afterthought (TechCabal, John Adoyi, 11 June 2025)

javascript.example: GDS measured over 500,000 visits and found that 1.1% of people (about 1 in 93) did not get the site's JavaScript, and most of them had JavaScript switched on but the scripts still failed to run (for example because of network errors on mobile). This is why a page's core job should not depend on JavaScript working.
javascript.source_title: How many people are missing out on JavaScript enhancement? (GDS blog, 21 October 2013)

javascript.example: Paystack publishes a small sample checkout where plain HTML forms plus JavaScript files (main.js and app.js) take card details, talk to your backend to start a transaction, and ask the backend to verify the payment afterwards. It warns developers not to give the card fields a name attribute so card details are never sent to their own server by mistake.
javascript.source_title: PaystackHQ/PaystackJS-Sample-code: Barebones Checkout using PaystackJS (GitHub README)

javascript.example: Airbnb publishes its JavaScript Style Guide, "a mostly reasonable approach to JavaScript", and matching ESLint rule packages so a whole team writes code the same way and tools can check it automatically. Many companies and learners reuse it as their own coding standard.

typescript.example: Stripe converted the code of its Dashboard, more than 3.7 million lines, from Flow to TypeScript in a single pull request in March 2022 after about a year of preparation. Engineers had asked for TypeScript because the old type checker was slow and used so much memory it could freeze their laptops.
typescript.source_title: Migrating millions of lines of code to TypeScript (Stripe, 20 May 2022)

typescript.example: Slack adopted TypeScript for its desktop app, where a small mistake can crash the whole application. While converting their code they were surprised by how many small bugs TypeScript found, such as misspelled property names and assuming a nested object always exists.

Flutterwave's official React library for accepting payments is written in TypeScript (files such as types.ts, useFW.tsx and FWButton.tsx), and its Angular, Vue and React Native libraries are also TypeScript. Types describe exactly which payment settings (amount, currency, customer) a developer must pass, so mistakes show up in the editor before customers see them.

react.example: In 2015 Netflix moved its website UI to React because it needed faster start-up, smooth runtime performance and modular code for running many A/B tests at once. React let it render the first screen on the server and then continue in the browser, and its virtual DOM reduced slow DOM updates.

GitHub rebuilt its code view in React to change the interface faster, but very long files became slow: the first render of an 18,000-line file took nearly 27 seconds. By only rendering the lines visible on screen (virtualization) and avoiding unnecessary re-renders, they brought it under one second.
react.source_title: Crafting a better, faster code view (GitHub Blog, 21 June 2023)

react.example: Flutterwave offers a React library with a useFlutterwave hook: a developer passes a config (amount, currency such as NGN, payment options like card, mobile money and USSD) and a button click opens the payment modal. It shows how African payment companies ship ready-made React components so web teams can take payments quickly.
react.source_title: Flutterwave/React-v3: Flutterwave v3 React Library (GitHub README)

rest_apis.example: PayPal built its busy account overview page twice, in Java and in Node.js, and the Node.js version was built almost twice as fast by fewer people with 33% fewer lines of code. It also served double the requests per second and pages about 200 ms faster, so PayPal decided to build its consumer web apps on Node.js.
rest_apis.source_title: Node.js at PayPal (PayPal Technology Blog, 22 November 2013)

rest_apis.example: Paystack's team built a Node.js and Express bot that reads songs staff share in a Slack channel, builds a monthly Spotify playlist with custom cover art and saves it to a MongoDB database. It is a small, real backend that glues several APIs together, with secrets kept in a .env file.

Flutterwave's docs show a Node.js server checking a payment with its official flutterwave-node-v3 package, reading the secret key from process.env. The server confirms the status, reference, currency and amount before giving the customer value, which is work that must happen on the backend, not in the browser.

Stripe's API lets clients send an idempotency key with each POST request, so if the network fails the client can safely retry and the customer is charged only once. Stripe also advises waiting longer between each retry (exponential backoff) with some randomness so servers are not flooded.
rest_apis.source_title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe Blog)

rest_apis.example: MTN's MoMo developer portal offers "Get paid" APIs (request payment, refund, payment status, account balance) and "Pay" APIs (transfer, transfer status) for businesses. A developer can build against a sandbox test environment before going live.

After a payment, Flutterwave tells developers to call its verify-transaction endpoint with the transaction ID in the URL and check the reference, status, currency and amount before giving value. The JSON response shows a typical REST pattern: a status, a message and a data object.

sql.example: GitHub upgraded more than 1,200 MySQL database hosts (300+ TB of data, 5.5 million queries per second) from MySQL 5.7 to 8.0 over about a year. They ran both versions side by side in CI, upgraded replicas one at a time and kept a way to roll back without downtime.
sql.source_title: Upgrading GitHub.com to MySQL 8.0 (GitHub Blog, 7 December 2023)

sql.example: Figma started in 2020 on a single Postgres database, and as it grew almost 100x it first moved groups of related tables into separate databases, then split very large tables (terabytes, billions of rows) across many databases (horizontal sharding). They chose to build on their existing Postgres because it was lower risk than adopting a new database.
sql.source_title: How Figma's Databases Team Lived to Tell the Scale (Figma Blog, 14 March 2024)

sql.example: Moniepoint moved important business logic from a live system handling millions of transactions to a new service with its own Postgres database, and refused to switch over until the new data was proved 99.9% accurate. They compared records in both systems continuously and with batch jobs, and tracked an accuracy rate on dashboards.
sql.source_title: Building Trust During System Migration: How We Reached for 99.9% Data Accuracy (Moniepoint Engineering)

git.example: Google's public code review guide says reviewers should approve a change once it definitely improves the overall health of the code, even if it is not perfect, because "there is no such thing as 'perfect' code". Review is about steady improvement, not blocking people.
git.source_title: The Standard of Code Review (Google eng-practices)

git.example: GDS uses GitHub pull requests so code is reviewed before it is merged, and reviewers check purpose, tests, security and documentation. They are told to give positive feedback, explain the reasons for suggestions, not rush reviews, and only approve changes they fully understand.
git.source_title: How to review code (The GDS Way)

git.example: Ushahidi's open-source platform asks contributors to fork the repository, work on a feature branch, open a pull request and include a checklist explaining how to test the change. Admins then review the code and either merge it, with credit to the contributor, or ask for changes pushed to the same branch.
git.source_title: Workflow for adding code (ushahidi/platform docs on GitHub)

testing.example: At GitHub, 1 in 11 commits used to have a failed build caused by a flaky test (a test that passes and fails on the same code). They built a system that retries failures to detect flakiness and assigns fixes to the right people, cutting this to 1 in 200 commits.
testing.source_title: Reducing flaky builds by 18x (GitHub Blog, 16 December 2020)

testing.example: Flutterwave gives developers a test mode with test cards, mobile money details and special OTPs so they can simulate successful and failed payments before going live. For example, special OTP codes trigger errors like "wrong OTP" or "insufficient funds" so you can test how your app handles them.

Moniepoint, which serves over 10 million businesses and individuals, requires every non-trivial change to pass automated unit, integration and end-to-end tests before it is merged. Every new service must also pass a documented load test before going to production, because "intuition is not evidence".
testing.source_title: High Availability in Production: What Running at Scale Actually Requires (Moniepoint Engineering)

security.example: GitHub required everyone who contributes code on GitHub.com to turn on two-factor authentication (2FA), rolled out gradually from March 2023, to protect against account takeover. Nearly 95% of affected contributors enrolled and overall 2FA adoption rose 54%.
security.source_title: Securing millions of developers through 2FA (GitHub Blog, 24 April 2024)

security.example: Webhook endpoints are public, so Flutterwave lets merchants set a secret hash, stored as an environment variable, and sends it in a verif-hash header. Your server must reject any request where the header is missing or does not match, so fake 'payment successful' messages cannot trick it.

MoMo API calls need a subscription key plus an OAuth 2.0 bearer token obtained with an API User and API Key. The token expires and "must be treated as a credential and kept secret", so apps request a new one before the old one expires.
security.source_title: API User and Key Management (MTN MoMo Developer Portal)

flutter.example: In 2020 Shopify decided to build all new mobile apps with React Native, because its web developers already knew React and teams felt about twice as productive. Two apps shared 95% and 99% of their code between iOS and Android.
flutter.source_title: React Native is the Future of Mobile at Shopify (Shopify Engineering, 29 January 2020)

flutter.example: Klasha, a startup connecting Africans to global goods and services, built its app with Flutter. The Flutter showcase says this helped it grow to more than 300,000 active users.
flutter.source_title: Klasha: Connecting Africa to the world with Flutter (flutter.dev showcase)

flutter.example: Nubank, a digital bank with over 48 million customers, compared Kotlin Native, React Native and Flutter and chose Flutter so features could launch on iOS and Android together. Flutter pull requests merge in about 9.9 minutes on average versus 70 minutes across all platforms, and new engineers contribute within days.
flutter.source_title: Scaling with integrity at Nubank with Flutter (flutter.dev showcase)

performance.example: Nearly two-thirds of Nigerian users go online over 2G and data is expensive, so Konga built a Progressive Web App that works offline. It used 92% less data than the native app for the first load and 84% less than the old mobile site to complete a first purchase.
performance.source_title: Konga cuts data usage 92% with new Progressive Web App (web.dev case study)

performance.example: Many Jumia users are on 2G, have data limits and basic phones, so Jumia built a lightweight Progressive Web App. Compared with its earlier mobile site it saw a 33% higher conversion rate and 50% lower bounce rate, and the PWA needed 25x less device storage.
performance.source_title: Jumia sees 33% increase in conversion rate, 12X more users on PWA (web.dev case study)

performance.example: Facebook started "2G Tuesdays": on Tuesdays staff are offered the chance to use the app on a simulated slow 2G connection, where a page can take minutes to load. This helps engineers feel what users in emerging markets experience and find problems to fix.
performance.source_title: Building for emerging markets: The story behind 2G Tuesdays (Engineering at Meta, 27 October 2015)

ci_cd.example: GOV.UK switched about 50 apps from manual deploys to continuous deployment: a reviewed change that passes automated tests goes to Integration, then Staging, then live, and stops if any test fails. The average time from test environment to live fell from 3 days to half a day, with no incidents caused by the change.
ci_cd.source_title: How and why we switched to Continuous Deployment on GOV.UK (Inside GOV.UK, 5 August 2021)

ci_cd.example: GitHub deploys tens of times a day, even on Fridays, to Kubernetes clusters and bare-metal servers. Deploys are automatically halted before problems reach customers, using checks such as Kubernetes readiness probes.
ci_cd.source_title: Deployment reliability at GitHub (GitHub Blog, 3 February 2021)

ci_cd.example: Paystack's open-source music bot has a CircleCI pipeline that, on every build, starts Node.js and a MongoDB test database, installs dependencies, runs the linter and runs the test suite. It is a small, readable example of continuous integration a beginner can copy.

problem_solving.example: In January 2017 an engineer meant to wipe a broken backup database but ran the command on the main database, deleting about 300 GB; GitLab lost around 6 hours of data (about 5,000 projects) and was down for many hours. The regular backups had been silently failing because of a version mismatch and failure emails were being rejected, which taught them to test restores and give backups an owner.
problem_solving.source_title: Postmortem of database outage of January 31 (GitLab Blog, 10 February 2017)

problem_solving.example: On 2 July 2019 a single badly written regular expression in a firewall rule used up the CPUs on Cloudflare's servers worldwide, causing 502 errors for 27 minutes. They fixed it by switching the feature off globally, then added CPU checks to their tests and staged rollouts so one change cannot reach every server at once.
problem_solving.source_title: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019 (Cloudflare Blog)

problem_solving.example: On 12 November 2018 a configuration mistake at Nigerian internet provider MainOne leaked network routes, sending Google traffic through Russia, China and Nigeria and making Google unreachable for many users for 74 minutes. The lesson was "too much trust and not enough verification": networks accepted the wrong routes without checking them.
problem_solving.source_title: How a Nigerian ISP Accidentally Knocked Google Offline (Cloudflare Blog)

typical.name: Recruiter screen
typical.what_happens: A recruiter calls you for 20-30 minutes to check your background, motivation, availability and communication. They also explain the steps that follow.
typical.how_to_prepare: Practise a two-minute story of who you are, what you have built and why this company. Read the job advert and prepare one or two questions of your own.

typical.name: Online coding assessment
typical.what_happens: You solve one or more timed coding problems alone on a platform, sometimes with a short work-style questionnaire. Automated tests usually score your answers.
typical.how_to_prepare: Practise small timed problems on arrays, strings and objects in your main language, and read the platform's rules before starting. Find a quiet place, check your internet and leave extra time.

typical.name: Live coding / pair programming
typical.what_happens: You write code with an engineer watching or pairing with you, often in a shared editor, on a small realistic task. They care about how you think, communicate and test, not only the final answer.
typical.how_to_prepare: Practise talking aloud while you code and asking clarifying questions before you start. Aim for a simple working solution first, then improve it and add tests or edge cases.

typical.name: Take-home exercise
typical.what_happens: You build a small program in your own time and tools, then submit it as a repository or pull request. A review call often follows where you walk through your choices.
typical.how_to_prepare: Keep it simple, readable and tested, and write a README explaining how to run it and what trade-offs you made. Stay within the suggested time and be ready to explain every line.

typical.name: System design (lite)
typical.what_happens: You sketch how a simple app would work, for example its pages, API endpoints, database tables and what happens when many users arrive. For junior roles it is a conversation, not a test of expert knowledge.
typical.how_to_prepare: Practise drawing a browser-server-database diagram for an app you built and explaining each part. Learn the basic words: API, database, cache, queue and trade-off.

typical.name: Code review exercise
typical.what_happens: You read someone else's pull request or merge request, leave comments and sometimes fix it live with an interviewer. They look at whether you spot bugs, missing tests and unclear code, and how kindly you give feedback.
typical.how_to_prepare: Review classmates' pull requests on GitHub and practise writing clear, polite comments that explain why. Use a checklist: does it work, is it tested, is it readable, is it safe?

typical.name: Behavioural interview
typical.what_happens: Interviewers ask about real situations, such as working in a team, handling a mistake or learning something new. They want specific examples of what you did and what happened.
typical.how_to_prepare: Prepare four or five short stories from projects, using Situation, Task, Action, Result. Be clear about your own part versus the team's and what you learned.

typical.name: Final interview and decision
typical.what_happens: You may meet a hiring manager or senior leader for a final conversation about fit and expectations. A panel or hiring committee then reviews all the feedback and decides on an offer.
typical.how_to_prepare: Research the company's products and values and prepare questions about the team and how juniors are supported. Ask the recruiter for feedback whatever the outcome.

Systems design with an engineer on a hypothetical problem, using a sketching tool

Hiring committee reviews all feedback and decides on an offer and team
